newsitem.title: UK: ECB independence - analysts weigh the pros and cons.
newsitem.headline: ECB independence - analysts weigh the pros and cons.

text.p: The European Central Bank (ECB), which will dictate monetary policy for a large chunk of western Europe after currency union in 1999, is set to be insulated from political interference.

But how that will be achieved, and whether a bank charged with such awesome responsibility should be devoid of political input, are questions yet to be answered as union fast approaches, analysts said on Thursday.

"Being fiercely independent does not necessarily mean being apolitical," said Michael O'Hanlon, chief international economist at PaineWebber in London. "If you look at the Bundesbank for example, a lot of the central bankers at the top end of the Bundesbank have political leanings."

The question of an independent ECB was highlighted once again this week as Britain's opposition Labour Party revealed plans to reform the Bank of England, one of Europe's most prominent central banks.

The reforms fell far short of shifting the final say on monetary policy -- and interest rates -- to the Bank from the government and left Britain as one of the few countries in Europe without an independent central bank.

From Italy to Spain and Belgium to the Netherlands, most central banks are seen to be independent of political control or are changing their statutes in preparation for that requirement after European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
ECB statutes state clearly that neither the ECB, nor a national central bank or member of its decision making bodies, will be allowed to take instruction from politicians.
A single eight-year period of office for the directorate -- the executive board of the ECB composed of the president, vice-president and four others -- should also promote independence, analysts say.
The directorate, together with heads of member central banks, will form a governing council which will decide policy.
But it is unclear yet whether the ECB, like the Bundesbank, will pursue price stability as one of its policies, which many analysts say is critical to promoting independence.
The new central bank would have to keep the core inflation rate, for example, within a clearly defined target. The target would remain in place even as ECB members came and went.
"You get political independence by having a clearly defined target so the market can interpret what the response should be when the economy changes," O'Hanlon said.
It will be a difficult task to define such a target, even after economic conditions converge in Europe, because of the variety of tax structures and labour regimes, he added.
"Even with VAT (value added tax), which should be the easiest thing to harmonise, there is great disparity," he said.

Chris Golden, head of portfolio strategy and EMU expert for Nomura Research Institute in London, said the U.S. Federal Reserve does not have a targeting process, yet is regarded as one of the most independent central banks in the world,
Even with a clearly defined targeting process there is no guarantee policy would not get hijacked by the directorate or the president of the central bank, analysts said.

While the heads of the national central banks, representing the interests of their countries, will each get one vote on the governing council, debate will likely be led by the president as is the case now at the Fed or the Bundesbank, O'Hanlon said.
So how will individual countries promote their economic concerns and should there not be any democratic respresentation at the ECB at all?
Golden, at Nomura, said France's proposal for a stability council would provide some form of political input.
"It does two things. It informs the central bank of political worries and it lends an aura of democratic process which to be fair is remarkably lacking at the moement," he said.
Lorenzo Cogdono, chief economist at Bank of America in Milan, said a clear mandate, and stringent reporting policies would make the ECB more accountable.
"Independence is a good idea, providing there is a clear mandate, continuous testimony and more reporting," he said.
Analysts point to Fed chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony to the U.S. government's Senate banking committee on Wednesday as a model to emulate.
